title: Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile (Chee Chee)
summary: Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile, also known as Chee Chee and Elizabeth Bess Haile, was a Shinnecock tribal member whose public life included storytelling, museum work, Tribal Council service, land-rights advocacy, and oral-history preservation.
content:
Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile, also known as Chee Chee and Elizabeth Bess Haile, is documented as a Shinnecock storyteller, museum leader, Tribal Council member, land-rights advocate, and oral-history contributor. A cited July 2011 interview shortly after her eighty-first birthday places her birth in July 1930; the sources used here do not establish a death date.

She was the daughter of Henry Bess, known as Chief Thunder Bird, and Edith Bess, and she appears in Shinnecock community histories as a Museum Board member, tribal storyteller, elder, and oral-history contributor.4 Published sources document her cultural and tribal leadership but do not establish a complete chronology of her life.3

Names, Family, and Shinnecock Roots

A photograph caption in The History & Archaeology of the Montauk identifies her as Elizabeth Bess (Haile), daughter of Henry Bess and his wife Edith.4 Strong's 1997 work also captions a 1974 photograph of Chief Thunder Bird, Henry Bess, with his daughter Chee Chee.1 The same source identifies Chee Chee as Elizabeth Haile and lists her as Shinnecock, Tribal Council, Museum Board, and tribal storyteller.1

Shoemaker met Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile at her home on the Shinnecock Indian Nation Reservation in July 2011, shortly after Haile's eighty-first birthday. This supports a birth year around 1930; the cited sources do not establish the exact date or place.3

Haile described her connection to Shinnecock land through long ancestral presence and through family practices of digging oysters and clams and fishing local waters. The oral history ties her early life to Shinnecock waters, seafood, and the continuing relationship between homeland and daily knowledge.3

Cultural Stewardship and the Shinnecock Museum

In 1990, the Shinnecock community established a board of directors and staff to plan the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum on the reservation. The published account names Chee Chee (Elizabeth Haile) among the directors who monitored the project and served as liaisons with the outside community.2

The museum's early programs included a reservation nature trail, educational visits, traditional food, and storytelling. Strong's 1994 account specifically describes storytelling sessions presented by Shinnecock storyteller Elizabeth Haile for groups that included Boy Scouts and a tour organized by the American Museum of Natural History.2

By the time Shoemaker interviewed her in 2011, Haile was described as a long active supporter of the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum and as its vice president.3 This places her public work within both preservation and teaching: collecting, interpreting, and passing Shinnecock history to Native and non-Native audiences.

Tribal Council and Shinnecock Land Advocacy

Published sources identify Haile as a member of the Shinnecock Tribal Council, which advised the tribal board of trustees.1 In a 1998 East Hampton Star article on Shinnecock land rights, she spoke publicly about recognition of Shinnecock original ownership, saying she wanted that ownership recognized and pointing to Shinnecock lands before 1859.5

That public statement connects Haile's biography to the long Shinnecock Hills land-loss history. It also shows her public leadership extending beyond museum interpretation into sovereignty, land memory, and the political work of naming Shinnecock dispossession in contemporary public forums.5

Oral History, Whaling, and the Sea

Nancy Shoemaker's Living with Whales includes oral histories from the Shinnecock Indian Nation, including Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile, Holly Haile Davis, and David Bunn Martine.3 The source explicitly identifies Holly Haile Davis as Elizabeth Thunder Bird Haile's eldest daughter, making the oral history intergenerational as well as individual.3

Haile's oral history connected Shinnecock life to seafood gathering, whaling memory, and the continuing importance of the ocean. Her reflections help explain why whaling history on Long Island is not only a labor or industry story, but also a Shinnecock cultural and spiritual history.3

Life Timeline and Places

The mapped path uses broad documented public locations: the Shinnecock Indian Nation Reservation, Shinnecock waters and bay context, the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum, Southampton/Shinnecock Hills land-rights context, and the public cultural-center fundraiser record.3265

Haile told Shoemaker that she had traveled widely and spent time with Native people across the continent. The cited interview does not identify a detailed route.3

Documented Scope

Published sources establish Haile's roles in Shinnecock cultural education, museum leadership, oral history, and land-rights advocacy. They do not provide a complete birth-to-death chronology.3

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island From Earliest Times to 1700 (1997), fig. 12.4 and identification index.
  2. John A. Strong, Long Island Historical Journal, Vol. 7, No. 1 (Fall 1994), discussion of the Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum planning board and educational programs.
  3. Nancy Shoemaker, Living with Whales: Documents and Oral Histories of Native New England Whaling History (2014), chapter 7.
  4. Gaynell Stone, ed., The History & Archaeology of the Montauk (1993), photograph caption identifying Elizabeth Bess (Haile).
  5. East Hampton Star, "Court - Shinnecock Land is Still Theirs" (1998).
  6. John A. Strong, We Are Still Here! The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island Today (1998), Shinnecock Nation Cultural Center and Museum fundraiser photograph and identification index.
